O gameplay é o grande foco aqui. O combate mistura pancadaria corpo a corpo com armas de fogo, mas o que realmente faz diferença é a agressividade. O jogo praticamente te recompensa por entrar no meio dos inimigos e resolver tudo da forma mais violenta possível.

As execuções são uma das partes mais marcantes. Você pode finalizar inimigos usando o cenário inteiro ao seu favor, esmagando, jogando em armadilhas ou simplesmente destruindo tudo na força bruta. Isso dá bastante impacto às lutas.

O combate corpo a corpo funciona surpreendentemente bem. Parry, esquiva e contra-ataque deixam as batalhas mais intensas do que só apertar botão sem pensar.

As armas de fogo ajudam a variar o ritmo, principalmente em áreas com muitos inimigos armados, mas eu senti que o jogo realmente brilha quando você parte pra pancadaria direta.

O ritmo é bem acelerado e quase não existe pausa. Você entra em uma sala, elimina todo mundo, segue pra próxima e repete o ciclo.

O que mais me pegou foi justamente essa sensação de brutalidade constante. Ele não tenta reinventar nada, só entregar ação visceral do começo ao fim.

Redeemer is a game built around raw impact—an unapologetically brutal top-down brawler that embraces the primal satisfaction of close-quarters combat while weaving a straightforward tale of violence and redemption. At its center is Vasily, a former operative who has withdrawn from a life of killing to live in quiet isolation among monks, only to be forced back into conflict when his past comes hunting for him. The premise is simple but effective, giving the experience a clear emotional anchor: you are a man trying to break from a life defined by violence, yet circumstances push you deeper into the brutality you hoped to leave behind. The story doesn’t try to surprise with twists or moral ambiguity; instead, it frames the action with a sense of personal struggle, turning each confrontation into a reminder of what Vasily is fighting against and for.

What carries the game moment-to-moment is its combat, which is fast, crude, and deliberately heavy. Redeemer mixes melee fighting, improvised environmental kills, and firearm skirmishes into a single energetic loop. Chains of punches and kicks flow into grabs and executions, and weapons—from axes to hammers to pistols and shotguns—can be picked up and discarded as the battlefield evolves. The top-down perspective gives a clear view of the chaos, letting you judge space, enemy clusters, and weapon placements as you carve a path through each arena. The controls are kept intentionally simple so that the immediacy of the action becomes the focal point. Every impact lands with a sense of weight, and the exaggerated finishers underscore the game’s commitment to visceral satisfaction.

The environments play a major role in keeping encounters intense. Many arenas encourage improvisation: smashing a foe against a wall, kicking them into machinery, grabbing nearby objects to extend combos. The level design occasionally shifts from tight interiors to wider industrial yards, but most spaces are built to funnel enemies toward you, forcing quick tactical decisions based on the tools at hand. The enemy variety isn’t vast, but the pacing ensures a steady escalation, with heavier units and ranged threats complicating encounters that would otherwise be too repetitive. These fights generate a certain rhythm—short bursts of brutality punctuated by brief lulls—that makes even a simple encounter feel like a miniature survival challenge.

Redeemer’s biggest weakness lies in its insistence on repetition. The formula, while initially thrilling, doesn’t always expand as the campaign progresses. The same types of rooms, enemy layouts, and kill opportunities can start to blend together, making long sessions feel more exhausting than engaging. Yet this repetitiveness is partially mitigated in the Enhanced Edition, which introduces improvements such as character class options, weapon upgrades, more balanced encounters, and the welcome addition of local co-op. These enhancements add variety and longevity, allowing players to tailor their approach and experience the game with a partner for a more energetic, chaotic flow.

Despite its limitations, Redeemer excels at delivering exactly the kind of catharsis it promises. The grim atmosphere, aggressive soundtrack, and gritty aesthetic amplify the tone of relentless combat, creating an experience that feels focused and unapologetic. It works best when taken as a short, intense journey rather than an extended campaign—something to be played in purposeful bursts, letting the momentum and violence remain satisfying rather than draining. It’s not a genre reinvention, nor is it a narrative heavyweight, but it is a tightly crafted homage to classic beat-’em-ups delivered with modern force.

For fans of hard-hitting action games who crave weighty combat, visceral animations, and a story that doesn’t get in the way of breaking bones, Redeemer remains a compelling choice. It is a game defined by impact—both in its gameplay and its portrayal of a man confronting the life he left behind—and while it may not impress through depth or complexity, it succeeds through raw, unfiltered energy.

[h2]Story[/h2]

Our hero is a man with a past that comes back to hunt him down, retired to a monk temple to start a new life, now he must fight back and kill those who destroy his present life.

[h2]Gameplay[/h2]

Redeemer is a brawler/beat 'em up with top-down view mechanics that offers simple gameplay with a variety of tools to achieve our goal. Martial arts is the main weapon we use, but once we get our hands on fire guns of all kind among other tools, that goes out the window.

Gameplay in general is quite barebones, but satisfying for the most part, it is brutal and bloody, rough around the edges. It is very weird as the game at some point forgets it is a beat 'em up and it turns into a shoot 'em up and we barely use our fists anymore as new and more advanced weapons start to show up. 

[h2]Graphics[/h2]

In terms of graphics Redeemer does not offer much, it feels like a PS3 game when it comes to effects, graphics in general, nothing out of the ordinary and horrible things like invisible walls that forbid you to enter certain areas. 

Same for effects, standard and nothing spectacular.

[h2]Sound and Music[/h2]

Not much to say here, run of the mill music and effects, voice acting is at least decent.

[h2]The Bad[/h2]

Redeemer is a fun game for what it offers, but the story and main plot are all over the place, it does a poor job at explaining what is going on, we fight normal enemy soldiers with weapons and suddenly we are facing all sorts of mutant monsters in a lab that goes on and on for multiple levels, all this leave you wondering at what point the revenge plot turns into a top down Farcry 1 game... seriously, it starts really good then the plot falls apart a little bit, it forgets it is a beat 'em up, it forgets about martial arts and it's all about new more murderous weapons, is this bad? well it depends on what you like and expect.

[h2]Conclusion[/h2]

Rough around the edges, decent graphics and sound effects Redeemer is a good time waster, a mindless game that will offer a good time of killing for a few hours, do not expect a groundbreaking game.
